paragraphs: Friend, here's what this passage teaches: God sees what was done, and He does not let it slide. Abimelech murdered his seventy brothers, and three years later everything looked settled. But the writer tells us God sent a spirit of animosity "in order that the crime against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come to justice" (Judges 9:24). Nobody gets away with it just because the dust settled and the calendar moved on.

Notice who gets repaid. It wasn't only Abimelech. The leaders of Shechem had helped him murder his brothers (Judges 9:24), and the passage ends with God bringing "all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads" (Judges 9:57). I think that's the part to sit with. Helping with the crime, cheering it on and taking the benefits of it all count in God's eyes, so we can't just point at the guy in front.

So why does it matter to you, baker? Because you can trust God to be just when things look unfair, and you don't have to be the one to settle every score. The passage says, "In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father" (Judges 9:56). Pay attention to who did the repaying, and let that settle your own heart. And the story of Gideon and Abimelech ends here, so you've seen it all the way through. That's why my ovens stay ready: the One we're baking for is righteous in every single thing He does.
